content_topics: Jump for height and distance (forward, backward, right and left),
learning_experiences: watch a video clip or a demonstration on jumping activities,
practise different ways of jumping with peers,
identify and collect locally available materials for improvising objects to be used in jumping while observing safety,
jump high for height and far in different directions,
collaboratively sing songs while jumping high and far in different ways,
talk about their own and others' performance in jumping activities.
key_inquiry_questions: Why are jumping activities important as a physical activity?
Which objects can be improvised for use in jumping activities?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: the learner improvises and creatively makes objects for jumping using locally available materials.
Communication and Collaboration: the learner talks about different ways of jumping with peers,
sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: the learner observes safety precautions when collecting appropriate materials for making uprights.
Unity: the learner cooperates with others while singing appropriate action songs as they jump high and far.
sub_strands.pcis:
Safety: the learner observes safety while collecting appropriate materials for making uprights to be used in jumping.
Self-awareness: the learner becomes aware of their ability to jumping high and far in different directions.

skills.name: Name ways of jumping and how to jump safely
skills.mastery: The child names ways of jumping (for height, for distance, forward, backward, to the right, to the left, over a rope or a line), says a jump takes off and lands on two feet with bent knees, and names one safety rule (land softly, jump on soft ground, leave space between children). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) improvise objects to be used for jumping; c) jump in different ways for coordination; d) sing songs while jumping for fun.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Jumping on two feet in play (pre-primary) comes before naming ways and directions of jumping. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Comparing longer and shorter (Grade 1 Maths) is used to tell a jump for distance. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls hopping on one foot a jump.

example.question: Is hopping on one foot the same as jumping on two feet?
example.correct_answer: no, a jump uses two feet

misconceptions.cause: Young children use "jump" for every bounce.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Jump on two feet, then hop on one, and look at the feet.
misconceptions.feedback: A jump takes off and lands on two feet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lands with straight, stiff legs.

example.question: How should your knees be when you land from a jump?

misconceptions.cause: The child does not feel the jolt as a danger.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "straight and stiff" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Land like a cat, quietly, with bent knees.
misconceptions.feedback: Bend your knees and land softly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up jumping for height and jumping for distance.

example.question: You jump as far forward as you can. Is that a jump for height or for distance?

misconceptions.cause: The child has not linked the words to the movement.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "for height" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Jump up to touch a leaf (height), then jump to a line far away (distance).
misconceptions.feedback: Jumping far forward is a jump for distance.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Jumps very close to other children.

example.question: Where should you stand when many children jump?

misconceptions.cause: The child likes to stay near friends.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "close to my friends" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stretch arms out: no one should be inside your space.
misconceptions.feedback: Leave space around you so no one gets hurt.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: identify and imitate objects that maintain a constant beat such as a ticking clock,
collaboratively tap/clap the beat using body percussion; clapping/tapping/marching/stamping the foot while singing simple songs,
watch live or recorded performances to identify body percussion accompaniments to songs,
explore their body and use body percussions to accompany familiar topical songs,
improvise body percussion accompaniments to songs,
record performances using a digital device or present to peers for feedback.

How can body percussions be used to create a rhythm?

Self-efficacy: the learner confidently accompanies songs using body percussion rhythmic accompaniment with peers.
Learning to learn: the learner identifies and keenly taps/claps the beat of a song.

outcomes.text: identify items that maintain a steady pulse for beat articulation
play a steady beat on a percussion instrument while singing
create a rhythmic accompaniment to a song using body percussion

skills.name: Identify things that keep a steady beat
skills.mastery: The child names things that keep a steady pulse (a clock ticking, walking feet, a heartbeat, a drum played evenly), tells a steady beat from sounds that come at uneven times (rain, people talking), and says a steady beat goes on evenly like walking. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) play a steady beat on a percussion instrument while singing.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Clapping along with a song (pre-primary) comes before naming what keeps a steady beat. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Naming familiar sounds (pre-primary) is needed to say which keep a steady beat. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Name the body percussion sounds
skills.mastery: The child names the body percussion sounds (clapping hands, tapping knees or the chest, snapping fingers, stamping feet) and says which body parts make each, and that body percussion can accompany a song by keeping its beat. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) create a rhythmic accompaniment to a song using body percussion.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Naming body parts (pre-primary) is needed to say which part makes each sound. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Feeling a steady beat comes before keeping it with body percussion. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Says rain on the roof keeps a steady beat.

example.question: Does rain on the roof keep a steady beat?
example.correct_answer: no, the drops come at uneven times

misconceptions.cause: Rain makes a repeated sound, so the child hears it as a beat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap with a clock tick, then try to clap with the rain.
misconceptions.feedback: A steady beat is even like a clock. Rain drops come unevenly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gets faster and faster while keeping a beat.

example.question: When you keep a steady beat, does it get faster?

misconceptions.cause: Excitement makes the child speed up.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, faster and faster" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk to the drum: do your feet speed up?
misconceptions.feedback: A steady beat stays even, like walking.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says people talking keep a steady beat.

example.question: Which keeps a steady beat: a ticking clock or people talking?

misconceptions.cause: Talking is a sound the child hears all the time.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "people talking" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap with talking, then with a clock.
misconceptions.feedback: A ticking clock keeps a steady beat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a steady beat must be loud.

example.question: Can a soft sound keep a steady beat?

misconceptions.cause: Drums are loud, so the child links beat with loudness.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it must be loud" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Tap a steady beat softly with one finger.
misconceptions.feedback: A soft sound can keep a steady beat too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls snapping fingers clapping.

example.question: You rub your thumb and finger to make a click. What is that?

misconceptions.cause: Both make a short sound with the hands.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "clapping" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap, then snap, and look at the hands.
misconceptions.feedback: A click with the thumb and finger is a snap.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says stamping is done with the hands.

example.question: Which body part do you stamp with?

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes the new words.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hands" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stamp your feet while saying "stamp".
misconceptions.feedback: You stamp with your feet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks you need an instrument to play percussion.

example.question: Can you play percussion with only your body?
example.correct_answer: yes, by clapping, tapping, snapping and stamping

misconceptions.cause: Percussion was shown with drums.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, you need a drum" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Play a song with claps and stamps only.
misconceptions.feedback: Your body can play percussion.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Claps whenever they like during a song.

example.question: When you clap along to a song, when do you clap?
example.correct_answer: on the beat, evenly with the song

misconceptions.cause: The child claps for fun, not in time.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "whenever I want" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk and clap together with the song.
misconceptions.feedback: Clap evenly on the beat of the song.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Lines; straight, wavy, zigzag and curved lines Direction; vertical, diagonal and horizontal,
learning_experiences: observe actual and virtual pictures and identify lines,
collaboratively, recognise straight, wavy, curved and zigzag lines within the environment,
select appropriate materials for drawing such as coloured pencils, crayons, and charcoal among others,
draw various lines; straight, wavy, curved and zigzag,
draw the lines in different directions; vertical, diagonal and horizontal,
create a pattern by drawing lines in different directions,
draw simple pictures using lines for enjoyment,
show and speak clearly about own and others’ drawing for feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: What tools are used in drawing?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: the learner draws lines in different direction; vertical, diagonal and horizontal.
Communication and collaboration: the learner speaks clearly about own and others’ drawing for feedback.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: the learner collaboratively, recognise straight, wavy, curved and zigzag lines within the environment
Responsibility: the learner cares for resources as they source appropriate materials for drawing such as coloured pencils, crayons, charcoal
sub_strands.pcis: Health promotion: the learner observes hygiene by properly washing hands after using found objects in the environment to draw.
sub_strands.links:
Mathematical Activities: the learner applies the line drawing skills acquired in Mathematics to draw various lines in the environment.
Environmental Activities: the learner names various lines in their environment.

outcomes.text: identify lines for familiarity
draw lines in different directions
draw patterns using lines in different directions
appreciate drawing pictures for expression

skills.name: Identify kinds of lines and their directions
skills.mastery: The child names straight, wavy, zigzag and curved lines, says the direction of a straight line (standing up: vertical; lying down: horizontal; slanting: diagonal), and finds each kind of line in objects around them (a door edge, a road, a snake, a fence). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) draw lines in different directions; c) draw patterns using lines in different directions.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Telling straight from curved lines (Grade 1 Maths) is the start of naming wavy and zigzag lines. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Holding a crayon and making marks (pre-primary) comes before drawing lines in named directions. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a wavy line a zigzag.

example.question: A line goes up and down smoothly like water. Is it a zigzag?

misconceptions.cause: Both lines go up and down.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw both: the zigzag has sharp points, the wavy line is smooth.
misconceptions.feedback: A zigzag has sharp points. A wavy line is smooth.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a line lying down vertical.

example.question: A line lies flat like the floor. What is it?

misconceptions.cause: The new words are easily swapped.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "vertical" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand up straight (vertical), then lie down flat (horizontal).
misconceptions.feedback: A line lying down flat is horizontal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a slanting line straight up.

example.question: A line slants like a ladder against a wall. What is it?

misconceptions.cause: It goes upwards, so the child calls it standing up.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "vertical" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Lean a ruler against a box and compare with a ruler standing up.
misconceptions.feedback: A slanting line is diagonal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a bent stick drawing is a straight line because it is a line.

example.question: Is the edge of a ball a straight line or a curved line?

misconceptions.cause: All lines seem straight to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "straight" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Run a finger round a ball and along a ruler.
misconceptions.feedback: The edge of a ball is curved.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Stretching positions (standing, sitting, kneeling and lying).
learning_experiences: talk about body parts involved in stretching,
demonstrate stretching in different directions with peers,
practise stretching in different directions,
practise stretching in different positions,
collaboratively, play appropriate games involving stretching while observing safety,
sing action songs on body parts involved in stretching,
team up to use digital devices to record performances on stretching for future reference.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is stretching important as a physical activity?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration: the learner actively talks about parts of the body that are used in stretching.
Creativity and Imagination: the learner creatively stretches in directions and in positions.
Digital literacy: the learner uses digital devices to record performances on stretching.
sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: the learner observes safety of self and others during stretching activities.
Love: the learner appreciates the ability of others stretching in different positions.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety and security: the learner stretches to a reasonable limit to avoid injuries while in different positions.
sub_strands.links: Environmental Activities: the learner stretches to different directions of the compass point.

outcomes.text: identify body parts involved in stretching
perform stretching in different directions for flexibility
enjoy stretching in different directions for body fitness

skills.name: Name the body parts and directions of stretching
skills.mastery: The child names the body parts that stretch (arms, legs, back, neck, fingers), the directions of a stretch (upwards, forward, backwards, sideways) and the positions (standing, sitting, kneeling, lying), and says a stretch is slow and held without bouncing. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) perform stretching in different directions for flexibility.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Naming the main body parts (pre-primary) comes before naming the parts that stretch. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Moving and standing still on request (pre-primary) is needed to hold a stretch. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Bounces up and down to stretch further.

example.question: How do you stretch your legs safely?

misconceptions.cause: Bouncing looks like trying harder.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bounce up and down" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Reach slowly, count to five and hold.
misconceptions.feedback: Stretch slowly and hold. Do not bounce.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stretches forward when asked to stretch sideways.

example.question: Stretch sideways. Which way do your arms go?

misconceptions.cause: The word "sideways" is new.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in front of me" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand between two friends and reach towards each.
misconceptions.feedback: Sideways means out to the sides.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks you can only stretch standing up.

example.question: Can you stretch while sitting or lying down?

misconceptions.cause: Stretches seen at assembly are standing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, only standing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Do one stretch in each position.
misconceptions.feedback: You can stretch standing, sitting, kneeling or lying down.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a stretch should hurt to work.

example.question: Should a stretch hurt?
example.correct_answer: no; you feel a gentle pull, not pain

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it must hurt" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe actual and virtual environment to; identify materials and tools for painting and colouring,
apply colour within the pictures using dry media to represent colours of objects in the environment,
paint using a brush within the shapes of the picture on paper,
paint using fingers on a paper or fabric,
use sponge to paint within drawn forms on a paper or fabric, take note; clean hands after painting,
display the pictures and talk about them with your peers.
key_inquiry_questions: Which tools can be used in painting?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner identifies materials and tools for painting and experiments with different techniques like using fingers and sponges.
Creativity and Imagination: the learner colours pictures and experiments painting using fingers, brushes and sponge for enjoyment.
Self-efficacy: the learner gains confidence as they engage in painting using different tools and display their pictures.

Unity: the learner promotes a sense of unity as they engage in painting activities with peers, collaboratively shares ideas, and appreciate each other's artwork.

sub_strands.links: Mathematics Activities: the learner applies the skill of counting to mix paint and paint using a brush within the shapes of the picture on paper.

skills.name: Identify materials and tools for painting and colouring
skills.mastery: The child sorts what is used up (materials: paper, fabric, paints, crayons) from what helps them work (tools: brushes, sponges, a palette), names each, and names the colours of things around them to colour them as they look (green leaves, a blue sky, brown soil). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) colour a picture to immitate the environment.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Naming the basic colours (pre-primary) is needed to colour things as they look. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Holding a crayon or brush (pre-primary) comes before naming materials and tools. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Say how to paint with a brush, fingers and a sponge
skills.mastery: The child says how each way of painting is done (a brush: dip the tip and stroke; fingers: dip one finger and dab or drag; a sponge: dip, press and lift) and which mark each makes (lines, dots, soft patches), and says hands and tools are washed afterwards. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) paint shapes using a brush; d) paint using fingers on a surface; e) paint using a sponge on a surface.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Knowing the tools comes before saying how each is used. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Making marks with a crayon or brush (pre-primary) comes before painting shapes. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

example.question: A man sings a low note loudly. Is it high or low?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "high, because it is loud" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing a low note loudly and a high note softly.
misconceptions.feedback: Loud is volume. High and low is pitch. A loud note can be low.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a fast song loud.

example.question: A song is sung quickly and softly. Is it loud?

misconceptions.cause: Fast songs often feel loud.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it is fast" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing fast and soft, like a whisper race.
misconceptions.feedback: Fast is speed. It can still be soft.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks big animals make high sounds.

example.question: Which makes a lower sound: a cow or a chick?

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up high and low.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a chick" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Moo low and cheep high.
misconceptions.feedback: A cow makes a low sound. A chick makes a high sound.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a slow song soft.

example.question: A song is slow and loud. Is it soft?

misconceptions.cause: Slow songs are often lullabies.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, because it is slow" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing slowly but strongly.
misconceptions.feedback: Slow is speed. It can still be loud.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says every fast song is angry.

example.question: A fast, bouncy song is about playing. What mood is it?

misconceptions.cause: Fast movement can look like anger to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "angry" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Dance to the song: does it feel angry or happy?
misconceptions.feedback: A fast, bouncy song often feels happy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Judges the mood only from one word.

example.question: A slow, soft song has the word "sun" in it. Is it exciting?

misconceptions.cause: The child picks out one known word.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, the sun is fun" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Listen with eyes closed: how does the music make you feel?
misconceptions.feedback: Listen to the music too. Slow and soft sounds calm.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says every slow song is sad.

example.question: A slow, soft lullaby. Is it sad or calm?

misconceptions.cause: Slow and sad are linked for the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sad" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing a lullaby to a baby doll and ask how it feels.
misconceptions.feedback: A slow, soft song can be calm, not sad.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names a mood but cannot say why.

example.question: Why does this song sound happy?

misconceptions.cause: The child is not asked for reasons at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "because" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: is it fast or slow? loud or soft?
misconceptions.feedback: Say why: fast and bouncy songs sound happy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe pictures of different water points at home and share with peers,
talk about water points at home,
talk about the dangers of water points at home with peers,
collect pictures of familiar water points from magazines, newspapers among others,
sort and cut out the pictures,
stick using glue side by side the pictures on a stiff paper to make a simple montage,
perform a singing game about the dangers of water,
show the montage work and talk about ways to be safe around water points at homes,
observe safety measures around water points at home by exercising self-discipline.

What materials are used to make a montage?

identify water dangers arising from water points at home
make a montage of water points around the home environment
narrate ways of applying safety around water points at home
appreciate water safety at home for life skills

skills.name: Recognise water points at home and their dangers
skills.mastery: The child names water points around the home (a tap, a water tank, a drum or jerrican of water, a basin or bucket, a well, a pond nearby) and the dangers each holds (drowning, even in a bucket for a small child; slipping on a wet floor; falling into a well). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G1.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: c) make a montage of water points around the home environment.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Sources of water in the immediate environment (Grade 1 Environmental Activities) name the water points at home. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Say how to keep safe around water points at home
skills.mastery: The child names ways to keep safe around water at home (never play in or near water without an adult, keep buckets, drums and wells covered, empty basins after use, walk on wet floors, call an adult if a little child goes near water). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Knowing the water points and their dangers comes before naming how to keep safe. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a bucket of water cannot be dangerous.

example.question: Can a baby be in danger near a bucket of water?
example.correct_answer: yes, a baby can fall in and drown

misconceptions.cause: Danger is linked only with rivers and the sea.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it is too small" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Talk about why a baby must never be left near a bucket.
misconceptions.feedback: Even a bucket can be dangerous for a baby.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a jerrican or drum of water is not a water point.

example.question: Is a drum full of water at home a water point?

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks water points are outside places.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, only rivers are" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count all the places water is kept at home.
misconceptions.feedback: A drum, a tank, a tap and a basin are water points at home.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not see a wet floor as a danger.

example.question: Water is spilt on the kitchen floor. What is the danger?

misconceptions.cause: Spilt water seems harmless.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "there is none" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk carefully on a wet floor in role play.
misconceptions.feedback: A wet floor is slippery. Someone can fall.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an open well is safe if you can see the water.

example.question: Is an open well safe to play near?
example.wrong_answer: yes, I can see the water
example.correct_answer: no, a child can fall in

misconceptions.cause: Seeing the water feels like being in control.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, I can see the water" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look at a picture of a covered and an open well.
misconceptions.feedback: An open well is dangerous. Do not play near it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is fine to play in a basin of water alone.

example.question: Can a small child play in water without an adult?
example.correct_answer: no, always with an adult near

misconceptions.cause: Water play is fun and seems safe.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play asking an adult before water play.
misconceptions.feedback: Always play in water with an adult near.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the lid off the water drum.

example.question: You take water from the drum. What do you do after?

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see a danger in an open drum.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "leave the lid off" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: who could fall in or what could get in?
misconceptions.feedback: Put the lid back on after taking water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Runs on a wet floor.

example.question: The bathroom floor is wet. How do you walk?

misconceptions.cause: Running feels quicker.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "run quickly" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Watch a toy slide on a wet tray.
misconceptions.feedback: Walk slowly on a wet floor.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not tell an adult when a baby goes near water.

example.question: Your baby brother crawls to a basin of water. What do you do?

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the baby is only playing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "nothing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play calling an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Call an adult at once.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

readiness.name: Move the body in basic ways
readiness.what: Walks, runs, jumps on two feet and stands still on request in a play area, and stops on a signal (a whistle or a clap).

readiness.name: Name the main body parts
readiness.what: Names and points to the head, neck, shoulders, arms, hands, back, tummy, legs, knees and feet.

readiness.name: Clap along with a song
readiness.what: Claps or taps along with a familiar song or rhyme, roughly in time with the group.

readiness.name: Sing simple songs and rhymes with actions
readiness.what: Sings simple songs and rhymes with the group and does the actions that go with them.

readiness.name: Name familiar sounds
readiness.what: Names familiar sounds (a cow, a dog, a car hooter, a bell, a baby crying) and says if a sound is loud or soft.

readiness.name: Name the basic colours
readiness.what: Names and points to red, yellow, blue, green, black and white in objects around them.

readiness.name: Hold a crayon and make marks
readiness.what: Holds a crayon, pencil or brush and makes marks, scribbles and simple lines on paper.

readiness.name: Handle soft materials
readiness.what: Tears paper, rolls and squeezes clay or dough, and folds a sheet of paper in half.

readiness.name: Play with a big ball
readiness.what: Rolls and tosses a big soft ball to a partner and stops a ball rolled to them.

readiness.name: Stay near a trusted adult
readiness.what: Knows to stay near a trusted adult at home and to call an adult when hurt, lost or afraid.
